claim: The study profiled chromatin accessibility in 25,613 individual cells from mouse perinatal testis after quality control filtration and doublet removal.
source: Altogether, we profiled chromatin accessibility in 25,613 individual cells after stringent quality control filtration and heterotypic doublet removal (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of cells profiled after quality control procedures.

claim: scATAC-Seq samples showed no clustering based on technical covariates such as TSS enrichment and number of fragments detected.
source: These samples showed no clustering based on covariates such as transcription start site (TSS) enrichment and number of fragments detected (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The manuscript states this observation and references a figure showing the data.

claim: Primordial germ cells give rise to M-prospermatogonia at about embryonic day 12.
source: Primordial germ cells give rise to M-prospermatogonia at about embryonic day (E) 12, which enter G0 mitotic arrest at about E14 to form T1-prospermatogonia (T1-ProSG) (McCarrey, 2013).
evidence: The manuscript cites McCarrey, 2013 as the source for this developmental timeline.

claim: M-prospermatogonia enter G0 mitotic arrest at about E14 to form T1-prospermatogonia.
source: Primordial germ cells give rise to M-prospermatogonia at about embryonic day (E) 12, which enter G0 mitotic arrest at about E14 to form T1-prospermatogonia (T1-ProSG) (McCarrey, 2013).
evidence: The manuscript cites McCarrey, 2013 as the source for this developmental timeline.

claim: T1-ProSG resume mitotic activity shortly after birth and migrate from the center of testis cords to the basal lamina.
source: Shortly after birth, T1-ProSG resume mitotic activity and begin migrating from the center of the testis cords to the basal lamina of testicular cords, and become T2-prospermatogonia (T2-ProSG).
evidence: The manuscript describes this developmental process without citation, suggesting it is established knowledge.

claim: T2-ProSG generate spermatogonia including self-renewing spermatogonial stem cells or directly transition into differentiating spermatogonia.
source: Once resident at the basement membrane, T2-ProSG generate spermatogonia including self-renewing spermatogonial stem cells (SSCs) or directly transition into differentiating spermatogonia that participate in the first round of spermatogenesis (Kluin and de Rooij, 1981; Manku and Culty, 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites Kluin and de Rooij, 1981 and Manku and Culty, 2015 as sources for this information.

claim: Sertoli cells actively proliferate during the neonatal period for 2 weeks in mice.
source: In mice, Sertoli cells actively proliferate during the neonatal period for 2 weeks (Vergouwen et al., 1991).
evidence: The manuscript cites Vergouwen et al., 1991 as the source for this information.

claim: PTMs are smooth muscle cells that distribute over the peripheral surface of the basement membrane.
source: PTMs are smooth muscle cells that distribute over the peripheral surface of the basement membrane (Maekawa et al., 1996).
evidence: The manuscript cites Maekawa et al., 1996 as the source for this characterization.

claim: PTMs are mainly involved in tubule contractions to facilitate sperm movement to the epididymis and secrete extracellular matrix materials.
source: They are mainly involved in tubule contractions to facilitate the movement of sperm to the epididymis and secrete extracellular matrix materials (Chen et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites Chen et al., 2014 as the source for PTM functions.

claim: There are two types of Leydig cells in mammals: fetal Leydig cells and adult Leydig cells, which develop sequentially.
source: In mammals, there are two types of Leydig cells, fetal Leydig cells (FLCs) and adult Leydig cells (ALCs), which develop sequentially in the testis (Shima, 2019).
evidence: The manuscript cites Shima, 2019 as the source for this information about Leydig cell types.

claim: Fetal Leydig cells start to degenerate after birth and are replaced by stem Leydig cells.
source: While FLCs start to degenerate after birth, they are replaced by stem Leydig cells (SLCs), which are the progenitors of ALCs (Su et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites Su et al., 2018 as the source for this developmental sequence.

claim: Stem Leydig cells are the progenitors of adult Leydig cells.
source: While FLCs start to degenerate after birth, they are replaced by stem Leydig cells (SLCs), which are the progenitors of ALCs (Su et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites Su et al., 2018 as the source for this lineage relationship.

claim: Only one previous study examined genome-wide chromatin accessibility in Sertoli cells using Sox9 transgenic line followed by DNase-Seq.
source: Notably, only one previous study examined the genome-wide chromatin accessibility in Sertoli cells, using the Sox9 transgenic line followed by DNase-Seq (Maatouk et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript cites Maatouk et al., 2017 as the only previous study examining chromatin accessibility in Sertoli cells.

claim: The study profiled chromatin accessibility landscapes of mouse perinatal testis across E18.5, P0, P2, and P5 by scATAC-Seq.
source: To delineate the dynamic changes on cellular populations in a developing testis, we profiled the chromatin accessibility landscapes of mouse perinatal testis across E18.5 and postnatal stages (P0, P2, and P5) by scATAC-Seq (Figure 1A).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the time points and method used for profiling.

claim: The time points E18.5, P0, P2, and P5 were chosen to represent the diversity of cell-type compositions involved in key developmental events in the testis.
source: These time points were chosen to represent the diversity of cell-type compositions involved in the key developmental events in the testis (Figure 1B).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the rationale for choosing these time points.

claim: Unbiased iterative clustering of single cells after integration identified 11 distinct clusters.
source: Unbiased iterative clustering of these single cells after integration identified 11 distinct clusters (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of clusters identified after integration.

claim: The study used Harmony to integrate datasets of four time points and project cells onto a shared embedding grouped by cell type rather than developmental stage.
source: To improve cell-type annotation, we used Harmony to integrate datasets of four time points and project cells onto a shared embedding in which cells were grouped by cell type rather than developmental stage (Korsunsky et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript cites Korsunsky et al., 2019 and describes the use of Harmony for integration.

claim: The vast majority of cells had a high prediction score and were confidently assigned to a single cell type.
source: The results showed that the vast majority of cells had a high prediction score and were confidently assigned to a single cell type (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: The manuscript states this result and references figures showing the prediction scores.

claim: Cell-type proportions varied across time points, such as the expansion of germ cells during the early neonatal period.
source: Cell-type proportions varied across time points, such as the expansion of germ cells during the early neonatal period (Figure 1E).
evidence: The manuscript states this observation and references a figure showing the data.

claim: The study identified 214,890 accessible chromatin regions in the scATAC-Seq library.
source: After identifying 214,890 accessible chromatin regions in the scATAC-Seq library (Supplementary file 2), we investigated cell type-specific chromatin accessibility profiles.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of accessible chromatin regions identified.

claim: Accessible sites are primarily located in the distal and intron region (>3 kb from TSS), suggesting an enrichment of gene regulatory elements.
source: Deconvolution of chromatin accessibility by cell types revealed that accessible sites are primarily located in the distal and intron region (>3 kb from TSS), suggesting an enrichment of gene regulatory elements (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The manuscript states this observation and provides an interpretation about regulatory elements.

claim: Cluster-specific DARs were associated with cell type-specific marker genes identified from scRNA-Seq.
source: We found cluster-specific DARs were associated with cell type-specific marker genes identified from scRNA-Seq (Figure 2B).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references a figure showing the association.

claim: Amh is a marker gene in Sertoli cells and showed increases in both number and amplitude of ATAC peaks within its promoter and gene body.
source: For example, Amh is a marker gene in Sertoli cells, and it showed increases in both number and amplitude of ATAC peaks within its promoter and gene body.
evidence: The manuscript provides Amh as an example of a marker gene with increased ATAC peaks in Sertoli cells.

claim: DNase I hypersensitive sites from bulk Sertoli cells were clearly enriched in the Sertoli cell population in scATAC-Seq.
source: We further compared DARs to a previously published DNase-Seq experiments in bulk Sertoli cells and found that DNase I hypersensitive sites were clearly enriched in the Sertoli cell population in our scATAC-Seq (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B; Maatouk et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript compares their data to Maatouk et al., 2017 and shows enrichment in Sertoli cells.

claim: ZEB1 and SNAI2 motifs were enriched in germ cells, indicating they may undergo mesenchymal-like transition in perinatal development.
source: For example, we found that ZEB1 and SNAI2 motifs were enriched in germ cells, indicating they may undergo mesenchymal-like transition in perinatal development (Hammoud et al., 2015; Liao et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript states the enrichment finding and provides an interpretation citing Hammoud et al., 2015 and Liao et al., 2020.

claim: Nuclear receptors NR4A1 and NR5A1 are enriched in Sertoli cells and Leydig cells.
source: Assessment of enriched TFs and their cognate motifs identified several known cell type-specific regulators – including the nuclear receptors (NR4A1 and NR5A1) in Sertoli cells and Leydig cells, ESR2 in Leydig cells, MYOG in PTMs, and previously uncharacterized TFs as potential cell type-specific regulators (Figure 2C).
evidence: The manuscript identifies these nuclear receptors as enriched in specific cell types.

claim: ESR2 is enriched in Leydig cells.
source: Assessment of enriched TFs and their cognate motifs identified several known cell type-specific regulators – including the nuclear receptors (NR4A1 and NR5A1) in Sertoli cells and Leydig cells, ESR2 in Leydig cells, MYOG in PTMs, and previously uncharacterized TFs as potential cell type-specific regulators (Figure 2C).
evidence: The manuscript identifies ESR2 as enriched in Leydig cells.

claim: MYOG is enriched in PTMs.
source: Assessment of enriched TFs and their cognate motifs identified several known cell type-specific regulators – including the nuclear receptors (NR4A1 and NR5A1) in Sertoli cells and Leydig cells, ESR2 in Leydig cells, MYOG in PTMs, and previously uncharacterized TFs as potential cell type-specific regulators (Figure 2C).
evidence: The manuscript identifies MYOG as enriched in PTMs.

claim: The study identified 35,245 peak-to-gene links by correlating accessibility changes of ATAC peaks within 250 kb of the gene promoter with mRNA expression.
source: We identified 35,245 peak-to-gene links by correlating accessibility changes of ATAC peaks within 250 kb of the gene promoter with the mRNA expression of the gene from scRNA-Seq.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of peak-to-gene links identified and the method used.

claim: 3262 peak-to-gene link regions overlapped with previously identified testis enhancers.
source: Some of these peak-to-gene links are likely to be promoter-enhancer regulatory units, as 3262 regions overlapped with previously identified testis enhancers (Gao and Qian, 2020; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The manuscript cites Gao and Qian, 2020 and states the number of overlapping regions.

claim: A region 13 kb upstream of Sox9 formed a peak-to-gene link with the Sox9 TSS, which is unique to the Sertoli cell population and overlapped with the TES enhancer including TESCO elements.
source: Comparison of the genomic region around Sox9 among all cell types revealed a region 13 kb upstream formed a peak-to-gene link with the Sox9 TSS, which is unique to the Sertoli cell population and overlapped with the 3 kb TES enhancer including the TESCO elements (Figure 3C).
evidence: The manuscript describes this specific peak-to-gene link and its overlap with known enhancer elements.

claim: The TESCO enhancer is a testis-specific enhancer that activates male-specific transcription of Sox9 during male sex determination.
source: During male sex determination, Sry activates male-specific transcription of Sox9 in the male genital ridge via the testis-specific enhancer core element (TESCO) enhancer (Sekido and Lovell-Badge, 2008).
evidence: The manuscript cites Sekido and Lovell-Badge, 2008 as the source for this information about TESCO.

claim: The analysis linked an additional three elements located 9 kb 5′, 21 kb 3', and 68 kb 3' to Sox9 representing novel regulatory elements.
source: Besides known enhancers, our data linked an additional three elements located 9 kb 5′, 21 kb 3', and 68 kb 3' to Sox9 representing novel regulatory elements of Sox9 gene regulation.
evidence: The manuscript identifies these as novel regulatory elements based on their peak-to-gene link analysis.

claim: The analysis successfully revealed a previously identified functional enhancer as a novel candidate to regulate Sertoli cell marker Wt1.
source: Our analysis also successfully revealed a previously identified functional enhancer as a novel candidate to regulate Sertoli cell marker Wt1 (Figure 3D).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references a figure showing the data.

claim: DLK1 is considered as a marker for immature Leydig cells in human.
source: Although DLK1 is considered as a marker for immature Leydig cells in human (Lottrup et al., 2014), the Dlk1-Gtl2 locus demonstrated preferential accessibility in stromal cells and PTMs.
evidence: The manuscript cites Lottrup et al., 2014 as the source for this characterization in humans.

claim: The Dlk1-Gtl2 locus demonstrated preferential accessibility in stromal cells and PTMs in mouse.
source: Although DLK1 is considered as a marker for immature Leydig cells in human (Lottrup et al., 2014), the Dlk1-Gtl2 locus demonstrated preferential accessibility in stromal cells and PTMs.
evidence: The manuscript states this observation from their scATAC-Seq data.

claim: Sorted DLK1+ mouse testicular cells showed higher expression of Igf1 mRNA compared to whole testis samples.
source: We sorted DLK1+ mouse testicular cells using fluorescence-activated cell sorting and observed higher expression of Igf1 mRNA compared to whole testis samples.
evidence: The manuscript describes their FACS experiment and RT-PCR results.

claim: Igf1 is commonly used as a marker for stromal cells.
source: This suggests that the sorted cells were enriched for stromal cells, since Igf1 is commonly used as a marker for this cell type (Figure 3F).
evidence: The manuscript states this as established knowledge about Igf1 as a stromal cell marker.

claim: Immunostaining of neonatal testis tissue demonstrated that stromal cells and PTMs were positive for DLK1.
source: Immunostaining of neonatal testis tissue demonstrated that stromal cells and PTMs were positive for DLK1 (Figure 3G).
evidence: The manuscript describes their immunostaining results and references a figure showing the data.

claim: Re-clustering of germ cells from the E18.5, P0, P2, and P5 testicular datasets revealed seven-cell clusters.
source: Re-clustering of germ cells from the E18.5, P0, P2, and P5 testicular datasets revealed seven-cell clusters (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of clusters identified in germ cell re-clustering.

claim: Germ cells from E18.5 and P0 are largely clustered together and occupy clusters GC1 and GC3, indicating minimal change of chromatin accessibility before and after birth.
source: Notably, germ cells from E18.5 and P0 are largely clustered together and occupy clusters GC1 and GC3, indicating a minimal change of chromatin accessibility before and after birth.
evidence: The manuscript states this observation and provides an interpretation about chromatin accessibility changes.

claim: The prediction revealed four clusters of known developmental stages: T1-ProSG, T2-ProSG, undifferentiated spermatogonia, and differentiation-primed spermatogonia, together with two clusters with unknown identity.
source: This prediction revealed four clusters of known developmental stages, T1-ProSG (T1), T2-ProSG (T2), undifferentiated spermatogonia (Undiff), and differentiation-primed spermatogonia (Diff), together with two clusters with unknown identity (Figure 4A).
evidence: The manuscript describes the cluster identities revealed by integration with scRNA-Seq data.

claim: The analysis identified 57 putative positive TF regulators in germ cell development.
source: We first identified the TFs important for each cluster, revealing 57 putative positive TF regulators in germ cell development (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of TF regulators identified.

claim: Foxo1 and Dmrt1 exhibited increased TF motif activity and gene expression in undifferentiated spermatogonia, consistent with previous studies.
source: For instance, consistent with previous studies, Foxo1 and Dmrt1 exhibited increased TF motif activity and gene expression in undifferentiated spermatogonia (Goertz et al., 2011; Matson et al., 2010).
evidence: The manuscript cites Goertz et al., 2011 and Matson et al., 2010 as previous studies supporting this finding.

claim: E2f4 shows highest activity in differentiation-primed spermatogonia and is known to be critical for the development of the male reproductive system.
source: E2f4 shows highest activity in differentiation-primed spermatogonia, and is known to be critical for the development of the male reproductive system (Danielian et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript cites Danielian et al., 2016 as the source for E2f4's role in male reproductive system development.

claim: Nr5a1 was identified as a positive TF regulator in the unknown germ cell clusters.
source: Interestingly, this analysis identified Nr5a1 as the positive TF regulators in the unknown clusters (Figure 4B and C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding from their TF analysis.

claim: A subset of germ cells expressed NR5A1, as confirmed by immunostaining.
source: Since Nr5a1 is widely considered as a somatic cell marker in testis (Luo et al., 1994), we performed immunostaining to examine NR5A1's expression in germ cells (Figure 4D). Indeed, a subset of germ cells expressed NR5A1, which ruled out the possible contamination from somatic cells.
evidence: The manuscript describes their immunostaining experiment confirming NR5A1 expression in germ cells.

claim: Previous scRNA-Seq of neonatal pro-spermatogonia identified a spermatogonial signature cluster showing high levels of mRNAs characteristic of Sertoli cells, including Nr5a1, Sox9, and Wt1.
source: Interestingly, previous scRNA-Seq of neonatal pro-spermatogonia identified a spermatogonial signature cluster showed high levels of mRNAs characteristic of Sertoli cells, including Nr5a1, Sox9, and Wt1 (Hermann et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites Hermann et al., 2015 as the source for this previous observation.

claim: The expression of the somatic cell marker WT1 has been observed in some germ cells through immunostaining.
source: Additionally, the expression of the somatic cell marker WT1 has been observed in some germ cells through immunostaining (Wen et al., 2021).
evidence: The manuscript cites Wen et al., 2021 as the source for this observation.

claim: Two possible differentiation trajectories were observed in germ cell development, with differentiation appearing to diverge at P0 via two distinct branches.
source: We then aimed to reconstruct the differentiation trajectories by ordering the clusters with developmental stages predicted by scRNA-Seq integration. Two possible trajectories were observed, as germ cell differentiation appeared to diverge at P0 via two distinct branches.
evidence: The manuscript describes their trajectory analysis results.

claim: The first trajectory represents differentiation from gonocyte to undifferentiated and then differentiating spermatogonia in P5, fitting the conventional model.
source: The first trajectory represents the differentiation fit into the conventional model as it charts a trajectory from gonocyte to undifferentiated and then differentiating spermatogonia in P5.
evidence: The manuscript describes this trajectory and its alignment with the conventional model.

claim: The second trajectory bypassed the undifferentiated state but passed through the unknown populations and directly reached the differentiating state by P5.
source: The second path bypassed the undifferentiated state but passed through the unknown populations and directly reached the differentiating state by P5.
evidence: The manuscript describes this alternative trajectory.

claim: The first round of spermatogonia arise from a unique Ngn3 negative pool of ProSG that transitions directly into A1 spermatogonia.
source: It has been reported that the first round of spermatogonia arise from a unique neurogenin-3 (Ngn3) negative pool of ProSG that transitions directly into A1 spermatogonia (Yoshida et al., 2006).
evidence: The manuscript cites Yoshida et al., 2006 as the source for this information.

claim: The unknown population (Unknown-2) displayed the lowest level of Ngn3 gene activity, raising the possibility that the second trajectory represents the origin of the first wave of spermatogenesis.
source: Interestingly, the unknown population (Unknown-2) displayed the lowest level of Ngn3 gene activity, which raised the possibility that the second trajectory represents the origin of the first wave of spermatogenesis (Figure 4E).
evidence: The manuscript presents this as a hypothesis based on the Ngn3 gene activity data.

claim: The motif binding activity of Id4 was initially high but then declined after birth, while that of ETS and Sp/KLF family members increased in spermatogonia.
source: We observed that the motif binding activity of Id4 was initially high but then declined after birth, while that of ETS and Sp/KLF family members increased in spermatogonia (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The manuscript describes these dynamic changes in TF motif activity along pseudotime.

claim: Sohlh2 is critical for early spermatogenesis and is more accessible at the late stage.
source: For example, Sohlh2, which is critical for early spermatogenesis, is more accessible at the late stage (Hao et al., 2008).
evidence: The manuscript cites Hao et al., 2008 as the source for Sohlh2's role in spermatogenesis.

claim: Ybx2 and Atf4 are both essential to male fertility.
source: This also raised some novel candidates regulating spermatogonial differentiation, such as Ybx2 and Atf4, which are both essential to male fertility (Fischer et al., 2004; Yang et al., 2005).
evidence: The manuscript cites Fischer et al., 2004 and Yang et al., 2005 as sources for the role of these genes in male fertility.

claim: The study predicted 12,819 putative peak-to-gene links in germ cells.
source: We further predicted regulatory interactions from scATAC-Seq data, identifying 12,819 putative peak-to-gene links (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of peak-to-gene links identified in germ cells.

claim: Re-clustering of Sertoli cells revealed six-cell clusters.
source: Re-clustering of Sertoli cells revealed six-cell clusters (Figure 5A).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of clusters identified in Sertoli cell re-clustering.

claim: SC1 is the most varied from the other Sertoli cell clusters, with marker genes related to spermatogenesis, such as Fzr1, Egfr, and Npas2.
source: SC1 is the most varied from the other clusters, with marker genes related to spermatogenesis, such as Fzr1, Egfr, and Npas2 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The manuscript describes the characteristics of the SC1 cluster.

claim: Gata2 and Ppara were enriched at early developmental stages in Sertoli cells.
source: For instance, Gata2 and Ppara were enriched at early developmental stages (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding from their trajectory analysis.

claim: Gata2 has been identified as a target of androgen receptor in Sertoli cells.
source: Gata2 has been identified as a target of androgen receptor (AR) in Sertoli cells, while Ppara regulates cholesterol metabolism and lipid oxidation in Sertoli cells (Bhardwaj et al., 2008; Shi et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites Bhardwaj et al., 2008 and Shi et al., 2018 as sources for these functions.

claim: Ppara regulates cholesterol metabolism and lipid oxidation in Sertoli cells.
source: Gata2 has been identified as a target of androgen receptor (AR) in Sertoli cells, while Ppara regulates cholesterol metabolism and lipid oxidation in Sertoli cells (Bhardwaj et al., 2008; Shi et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites Bhardwaj et al., 2008 and Shi et al., 2018 as sources for these functions.

claim: Hic1 and Cebpd were upregulated at the later stage of Sertoli cell development.
source: In contrast, Hic1 and Cebpd were upregulated at the later stage (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding from their trajectory analysis.

claim: Conditional knockout of Hic1 in mice resulted in fewer Sertoli cells in seminiferous tubules.
source: Conditional knockout of Hic1 in mice resulted in fewer Sertoli cells in seminiferous tubules (Uchida et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript cites Uchida et al., 2020 as the source for this information.

claim: Induction of C/EBP proteins by cAMP may play a role in FSH-dependent regulation in Sertoli cells.
source: Further, induction of C/EBP proteins by cAMP may play a role in FSH-dependent regulation in Sertoli cells (Grønning et al., 1999).
evidence: The manuscript cites Grønning et al., 1999 as the source for this information.

claim: The SC1 cluster could be clearly distinguished from other Sertoli cell clusters as 11 identified potential positive TF regulators either have highest or lowest activity in SC1.
source: Interestingly, the SC1 cluster could be clearly distinguished from the other cell clusters as the 11 identified potential positive TF regulators either have highest or lowest activity in SC1 (Figure 5D).
evidence: The manuscript describes this distinguishing characteristic of the SC1 cluster.

claim: Activity of several SP/KLF family members are enriched in SC1, including Sp1, which is reported to upregulate the transcription of nectin-2 and JAM-B in Sertoli cells.
source: For example, activity of several SP/KLF family members are enriched in SC1, including Sp1, which is reported to upregulate the transcription of nectin-2 and JAM-B in Sertoli cells (Lui and Cheng, 2012).
evidence: The manuscript cites Lui and Cheng, 2012 as the source for Sp1's function in Sertoli cells.

claim: SC1 is characterized by significantly higher gene activity of Amh and Mbd3 when compared with other Sertoli cell clusters.
source: SC1 is also characterized by a significantly higher gene activity of Amh and Mbd3, a 5hmC binding protein, when compared with other clusters (Figure 5E, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The manuscript describes this characteristic of the SC1 cluster.

claim: Immunostaining results confirm that MBD3-high cells tend to have higher levels of AMH.
source: Immunostaining results confirm the properties of SC1 cells as MBD3-high cells tend to have higher levels of AMH (MBD3-high/AMH-high).
evidence: The manuscript describes their immunostaining results confirming this relationship.

claim: SC1 cells showed lower gene activity of Sertoli cell markers Sox9, Dmrt1, and Wt1, as well as the lowest motif binding activity and gene score for FOS.
source: We also observed lower gene activity of Sertoli cell markers Sox9, Dmrt1, and Wt1 in SC1, as well as the lowest motif binding activity and gene score for FOS, a mediator of Sertoli cell differentiation (Figure 5E, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C) (Papadopoulos and Dym, 1994).
evidence: The manuscript cites Papadopoulos and Dym, 1994 as the source for FOS's role in Sertoli cell differentiation.

claim: SC1 cells might represent a less differentiated state of Sertoli cells.
source: Therefore, SC1 cells might represent a less differentiated state of Sertoli cells, which warrant further investigation (Estermann et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript presents this as a hypothesis based on their data and cites Estermann et al., 2020.

claim: Re-clustering of Leydig cells generated three main clusters.
source: Re-clustering of Leydig cells generated three main clusters (Figure 5G, Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of clusters identified in Leydig cell re-clustering.

claim: Cluster LC2 is likely to represent fetal Leydig cells, while LC1 and LC3 showed enrichment in different sets of stem Leydig cell markers.
source: Based on the gene activities of known Leydig cell markers, cluster LC2 is likely to represent FLCs, while LC1 and LC3 showed enrichment in different sets of SLC markers (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The manuscript describes the cluster identities based on marker gene expression.

claim: Most of the marker genes identified across Leydig cell clusters were upregulated in LC1.
source: Notably, most of the marker genes identified across the clusters were upregulated in LC1 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The manuscript states this observation about marker gene distribution.

claim: GO terms associated with the marker genes in LC1 include extracellular structure organization and connective tissue development.
source: GO terms associated with the marker genes in LC1 include extracellular structure organization and connective tissue development (Figure 5—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: The manuscript describes the GO enrichment results for LC1 marker genes.

claim: Col4a1 and Col4a2 showed higher gene activity in LC1, accompanied by LC1-specific peak-to-gene links to the bidirectional collagen IV promoter.
source: For instance, Col4a1 and Col4a2 showed higher gene activity in LC1, accompanied by LC1-specific peak-to-gene links to the bidirectional collagen IV promoter (Figure 5H).
evidence: The manuscript describes this finding from their peak-to-gene link analysis.

claim: Collagen IV-mediated signaling is involved in progenitor Leydig cell proliferation, suggesting that LC1 cells may represent a later developmental stage of stem Leydig cells.
source: Previous studies have indicated that collagen IV-mediated signaling is involved in progenitor Leydig cell proliferation, suggesting that LC1 cells may represent a later developmental stage of SLC (Anbalagan and Rao, 2004).
evidence: The manuscript cites Anbalagan and Rao, 2004 and presents this as an interpretation of their data.

claim: The study identified 40 putative positive TF regulators of Leydig cells.
source: Next, we identified 40 putative positive TF regulators of Leydig cells (Figure 5I).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of TF regulators identified in Leydig cells.

claim: Thyroid hormone receptors Thra and Thrb were upregulated in LC2 (fetal Leydig cells).
source: For instance, thyroid hormone receptors Thra and Thrb were upregulated in LC2.
evidence: The manuscript states this finding from their TF analysis.

claim: Re-clustering of PTMs and stromal cells generated 10 clusters.
source: Re-clustering of this cell group generated 10 clusters of cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A and B).

source: Within the clusters, PC8, PC9, and PC10 showed higher gene activity of Myh11, indicating their PTM identity, while other clusters were stromal cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C)
evidence: The manuscript describes the cluster identities based on Myh11 expression.

claim: The gene expression pattern of PC2 resembles telocytes, a recently described stromal cell type, which co-expresses Tcf21, Cd34, and Pdgfra and is negative for Pecam1, Kit, and Acta2.
source: Interestingly, the gene expression pattern of PC2 resembles telocytes, a recently described stromal cell type, which co-expresses Tcf21, Cd34, and Pdgfra and is negative for Pecam1, Kit, and Acta2 (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C; Marini et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites Marini et al., 2018 and describes the similarity to telocytes.

source: Motif enrichment analysis of DARs across clusters indicated that AR, PGR (progesterone receptor), and muscle-specific TF motifs were enriched in PTM clusters (Figure 5—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: The manuscript describes the motif enrichment results for PTM clusters.

claim: WT1 and SP family members exhibited higher TF motif activity in stromal cell cluster PC3.
source: In contrast, WT1 and SP family members exhibited higher TF motif activity in stromal cell cluster PC3.
evidence: The manuscript describes the motif enrichment results for stromal cell cluster PC3.

claim: 9 of the 46 TFs along the PTM developmental trajectory are homeobox genes.
source: Interestingly, 9 of the 46 TFs along the trajectory are homeobox genes.
evidence: The manuscript states this observation about the TFs identified along the trajectory.

claim: Hoxc6 is upregulated at the early stages of PTM development and has been implicated in steroid hormone regulation.
source: For example, Hoxc6 is upregulated at the early stages and has been implicated in steroid hormone regulation (Ansari et al., 2011).
